title: Explain the Union-Find / Disjoint Set data structure. How do find(x) with path compression and union(x,y) by rank achieve near-constant amortized time?
shortTitle: Explain Union-Find (Disjoint Set Union) — find with path compression, union by rank

s1_definition.profdef: Union-Find (Disjoint Set Union) maintains a partition of elements into disjoint sets, supporting two operations: `find(x)` returns a representative root of the set containing x, and `union(x, y)` merges the two sets. With path compression (flattening the tree during find) and union by rank/size (attaching the smaller tree under the larger), the amortized cost per operation is the inverse Ackermann function, effectively constant.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of National Bank of India grouping customer accounts into "related-party clusters." Each cluster has one head account. To ask whether two accounts belong to the same cluster, you walk up to each account's head and compare. Union-Find keeps those walks short by pointing accounts directly at the head once discovered, so repeated checks are almost instant.
s1_definition.oneliner: Union-Find tracks "which group am I in" with roots, and path compression plus union by rank make find and union almost O(1).
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Union-Find (Disjoint Set Union) maintains a partition of elements into disjoint sets, supporting two operations: `find(x)` returns a representative root of the set containing x, and `union(x, y)` merges the two sets. With path compression (flattening the tree during find) and union by rank/size (attaching the smaller tree under the larger), the amortized cost per operation is the inverse Ackermann function, effectively constant.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of National Bank of India grouping customer accounts into "related-party clusters." Each cluster has one head account. To ask whether two accounts belong to the same cluster, you walk up to each account's head and compare. Union-Find keeps those walks short by pointing accounts directly at the head once discovered, so repeated checks are almost instant.

**One line to remember:** Union-Find tracks "which group am I in" with roots, and path compression plus union by rank make find and union almost O(1).

sections.s2_technical:
The structure stores a `parent[]` array where each element points to its parent and a root points to itself. `find(x)` follows parent links to the root. For example: `while (parent[x] != x) x = parent[x]; return x;`.

Path compression rewrites the chain during find so future lookups are flat. For example, the recursive form `parent[x] = find(parent[x]); return parent[x];` makes every node on the path point directly to the root.

Union by rank keeps trees shallow. You find both roots and attach the lower-rank root under the higher-rank root; on a tie you pick one and increment its rank. For example: `if (rank[a] < rank[b]) parent[a] = b; else if (rank[a] > rank[b]) parent[b] = a; else { parent[b] = a; rank[a]++; }`.

A senior nuance is that path compression and union by rank together give the inverse-Ackermann bound, but either alone is weaker; and that union by size is an equally good alternative that also enables counting component sizes cheaply.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At National Bank of India, fraud analysts link accounts that share a device, phone, or address into related-party clusters. They repeatedly ask "are Rajesh's account SAV2001 and Priya's account CUR3001 in the same cluster?" This is exactly how Union-Find find works.

Problem 2 — As new shared signals arrive, two clusters must merge into one. This is exactly how union works, and union by rank keeps the lookups fast as clusters grow.

The mini-project builds a `RelatedPartyUnionFind` with path compression and union by rank, a `BankLogFormatter`, and a runnable demo.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is five accounts, initially five separate clusters.

Step 1: union(0,2) attaches account two under account zero; four clusters remain.

Step 2: union(1,3) attaches account three under account one; three clusters remain.

Step 3: connected(0,1) finds root zero for the first and root one for the second, so they differ and the answer is false.

Step 4: union(2,1) finds roots zero and one, merges them by rank, and drops the count to two clusters.

Step 5: connected(0,1) now returns the same root for both, so the answer is true; path compression flattened the chains during these finds.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Union-Find, also called Disjoint Set Union, maintains a partition of elements into non-overlapping sets and answers two questions extremely fast: which set does an element belong to, and merge these two sets. It stores a parent array where every element points toward a representative root, so find walks up to the root and union links one root under another.

The two optimizations are what make it fast. Path compression rewrites the path during find so every node on it points directly to the root, flattening the tree for all future lookups. Union by rank, or equivalently by size, always attaches the shorter tree under the taller one so the tree never grows unnecessarily deep. Together they give an amortized cost that is the inverse Ackermann function, which is effectively constant for any realistic input.

In my project at National Bank of India, fraud analysts needed to cluster accounts that shared a device, phone, or address and repeatedly ask whether two accounts belonged to the same related-party cluster. Union-Find was the natural fit: each shared signal triggered a union, each risk check was a connected query, and because the structure stayed flat the checks remained near-instant even as clusters grew into the thousands.
